items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: He and Duke Ellington had that same thing, and Basie was so honest.

ctx.x: And you had quite a wonderful association with Count Basie.

Oh, yeah. It was gorgeous. He was a great man. I mean he was great in such a quiet way. There wasn’t any flamboyance about him. What it was about him, I think was his magnetism. He just set still and was quiet. But nothing happened until he moved. I mean the band would be on the bandstand, and everybody would be sitting there and he’d come and make that introduction, and the whole band would come to life. He and Duke Ellington had that same thing, and Basie was so honest. You know he was such an honest man that…
Yeah there was some difference between how the English language was used between the London Times and —

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We went up to his suite in the Fairmont one night, just Judith and me. Duke talked to us all night long.

ctx.x: What kinds of things were you doing to hone your skills, technique-wise? Did you work with the piano at all?

No. I would just listen. Duke Ellington said the same thing. I was very relieved when I talked with Duke. We went up to his suite in the Fairmont one night, just Judith and me. Duke talked to us all night long. It was the most wonderful night that I ever spent, because he said a lot of things that I felt in my heart. He said – like, Judith had always been getting on me. When I had to write something, I would wait until the night before, and then suddenly, in a spurt of frenetic – what do you call it? . . .

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Well you know Duke did that too. He told me about that — where he’d meet these kids at these proms

ctx.x: Yeah. And I was also heartened and kind of amazed, because it both exhilarated Annie and me, but brought to my attention something that I try not to pay too much attention to which is age — the fact that I was entertaining three generations. People came with their © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

grown sons and daughters and their children’s records. They all had the albums. See it was three generations looking at us: grandpa and grandma, who were the big hard core fans forty years ago; their sons, 24, 25, out of college you know with their wives; and their kids, with the albums. And I said how old does that make me? It’s amazing. It really takes your breath away. It starts you to thinking, good Lord, that’s quite something. I think that’s really interesting. Well you know Duke did that too. He told me…

That was my son. Well when you look in jazz history there’s a small number comparatively of real innovators. There’s people that build on the innovations. I think that you’re one of those small number of innovators and gosh, you can take a great deal of pride in that.
